utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, and the best wishes from the Chamber to everyone for the year to come. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic. Please be seated. Mr. Pasic, first of all I would like to extend the wishes for 2006 from the Chamber to you as well. Best wishes. And I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Even if that was in 2005, it's still binding in 2006 as well. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, when we concluded your examination at the last session, we were discussing the expulsion of Muslims from the villages in the Japra valley that occurred on the 23rd and the 24th of May 1992, those villagers finding themselves sequestered in the village of Blagaj. According to the Defence Exhibit, D115, particularly page 9 of this exhibit in the English translation, negotiations regarding the status of the Muslim population were held with the organs of the ARK and the government of the Serb Republic of Krajina and UNPROFOR. And in respect of those negotiations you could only recall a single conversation that you had with Mr. Kupresanin. According to this Defence Exhibit 115 at page 10, the ARK government and the government of the Serb Republic were asked to determine a decisive stand on the status of the Muslims in Blagaj, and the answer that was given was that it was possible that they could be exchanged for Serbs captured elsewhere in Bosnia. You were unable in your evidence to identify persons in the government of the Serb Republic with whom you had discussions. The report concludes in respect of the people in Blagaj that "appropriate measures were taken to allow the people to move out in the direction of Banja Luka, which was done on the 8th of June." Now, in fact, Mr. Pasic, the public views of the leaders, the Bosnian Serb leaders in the ARK, including Mr. Kupresanin, was that Muslims should be expelled from the area. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's rather a long question, but what you said at the end, I have understood. Although that was not the case, that was not the position, and if you read the report carefully about the work of the Crisis Staff, which we had here, it said there that the possibility was just reviewed of a possible exchange. The possibility was looked into but the negotiations hadn't been completed, nor did anybody take a final decision on the matter. And as the war had flared up in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, I consider that possibility - and you only mentioned a portion of the possibility - as I say, the possibility was discussed, but it wasn't definitely adopted or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question I asked you was the public views of the ARK leaders was that the Muslims should be expelled. That was the public position taken by the leaders of the ARK, including Mr. Kupresanin. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that. I don't know that that was a public view, and I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Your Honours, to tab 16. This is a Prosecution Exhibit P187, and if that could be -- a copy of that could be provided to Mr. Pasic. I'm directing Your Honours' attention -- I will direct Your Honours' attention to subpart 5 on page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, for the record, the document that you will be shown, Prosecution Exhibit 187, is a military secret, a confidential report of the 1st Krajina Corps command, dated the 31st of May 1992. It is a regular combat report, and it was signed by General -- the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, Major General Momir Talic, and if I can direct your attention to page 5 -- to subpart 5 in the B/C/S, which is found with -- on page 2, I'm going to read a portion of this to you. "After the actions in Kozarac, Kljuc, and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from the units. They express their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns. The fact that Muslims and Croats who respond to the mobilisation, and conscripts of Serbian nationality who previously avoided military obligations are accepted into the unit with reluctance, has a most disadvantageous influence on the morale of the troops. This is made worse by public statements made in the media by SDS Bosanska Krajina autonomous region leaders who advocate the moving and expelling of all Muslims and Croats from these areas." Do you see that in this report, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Do I see what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see the portion that I read to you? I'll reread it to you: "This is made worse by public statements made in the media by SDS Bosanski Krajina --"

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "-- region leaders who advocate moving and expelling of all Muslims and Croats from these areas." Mr. Pasic, does that refresh your recollection as to the public comments that were made by the ARK leaders at the time the Muslims were sequestered in Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously -- I don't know if you understood my position and function at that time, the position I occupied. Now, if this is true, what you said, this is not a -- this couldn't have been a piece of information that was accessible to me, nor do I know anything about this piece of information, so I can't enter into the rightness or wrongness of what was written here, but let me repeat that I was not aware and informed of facts as they have been laid out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you participate in the negotiations with Muslim representatives who were sequestered in Blagaj, as to what would happen to them, as to where they would go?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how you mean "sequestered in Blagaj." They weren't sequestered in Blagaj. Blagaj is a village, it's an area where for a time from the other parts of the village parts of the Muslim population was located, and I negotiated with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you negotiate with Sifet Barjaktarevic, among others?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He made it clear, as did other representatives, that they wanted to return to their villages in the Japra valley. That was one of their positions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One of the positions of Sifet Barjaktarevic and Mr. Sefer Halilovic was that they wished to leave those areas for a number of reasons, the ones I discussed when we were here previously, their motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Pasic, that they never once expressed the desire to return to their homes in the Japra valley? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as far as I know, what they asked was to leave the area for a number of reasons and one of those reasons was the talk with Mr. Kirudja in present day Croatia in a place called Topusko where I think they negotiated on one occasion with Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The fact was, Mr. Pasic, that the Muslims were not going to be permitted to return to their homes; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn, Your Honours, to Prosecution Exhibit 739, it's found in tab 17. And Witness, if you could turn to tab 17, I want to refer you to a 1st Krajina Corps command report dated the 1st of June. It is authored by Colonel Milutin Vukelic. It's a report on the current political and security situation in the area. And, Witness, I'm going to read a portion of the third paragraph of this report. That is found on page 1 in the B/C/S and page 1 in the English, starting in the middle of the paragraph: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." That was the position of the political leadership in the ARK region. Isn't that the case, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't agree with this. And here is why: I have to tell you, and I said this last time, that otherwise we had very little contact when it came to Krajina and anybody else at the level of the republic. So positions of this kind are not something I'm aware of. I don't know that anybody had to leave because they were forced to leave when it came to the official organs at that time, so I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you participated in meetings with other regional representatives and conveyed the results of those meetings to the ARK Crisis Staff. In fact, you made demands as a result of meetings that you had, where you were present with representatives of other municipalities. Do you recall participating in such meetings, Mr. Pasic, in the month of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which meetings you have in mind. There were a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you participate in meetings with political representatives of other municipalities in the month of June where you discussed the situation of -- on the ground in your respective municipalities, including the situation in respect of Muslims and Croats who were living in your municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, throughout the months of May and June, there were difficult days for the Novi Grad municipality and Bosanski Novi, and I really don't remember -- well, I know that I spent most of my time in my office, in fact, and for objective reasons; because the security situation was such and you couldn't get to other municipalities that easily. So possibly there were, but I'm not sure I remember what meetings you have in mind and what they discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We could disseminate the next exhibit, it's a new exhibit, it's not found in the binders and it needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before doing so, Mr. Harmon, you referred us to tab 17 and I have difficulties in finding the quote you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 17, Your Honour, it is found in the third paragraph, in the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 17, I have -- I have no third paragraph where I could find in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be a document 1st Krajina Corps dated June the 1st, in tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not there. I've got a document the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. I will make -- then if we can return to that document, Your Honour, I will make sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you please, so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Exhibit 739, so I will make sure there are copies distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Pasic. It is entitled --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the accused have one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is entitled Inter-Municipal Agreements in the Sana-Una area, Korcanica, 14th of June 1992 at 1200 hours. Present are representatives of Bosanska Krupa [sic], Bosanski Petrovac, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, and Sanski Most, and you'll see a list of topics. And this was a meeting that you attended, Mr. Pasic. If you turn to the last page of this document, you will see a handwritten list of people who attended the meeting, and if you direct your attention, Mr. Pasic, to number 11, is that your name and signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my name and signature, but I never attended that meeting. I don't remember attending -- at being at Korcanica at all. I think it's a place on Mount Grmac [phoen]. However, I was never there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why don't you cast an eye very briefly, because we are going to be turning to another document in a minute -- why don't you cast your eye very quickly to the content of this document and see if this refreshes your recollection. And cast your eye, also, Mr. Pasic, to the other attendees, who include Mr. Rasula, number 2; Mr. Anicic, number 3; Simo Drljaca, number 13; Vlado Vrkes, number 21. See if the list of attendees and the substance of this refreshes your recollection.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't remember ever having been at Korcanica. There were meetings which were held in Sanski Most and I do remember some of those meetings. However, the meeting at Korcanica, I really don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn now to another exhibit and then, Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not yet given a number to the document you just presented to the witness. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1030, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 18, Mr. Pasic, tab 18 is a document, it's a Prosecution Exhibit P192, also P529 Hanson tab 343. This is a document dated the 7th of June 1992, Sanski Most, and it's conclusions that were adopted at a subregional meeting of political representatives of the municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc. And these conclusions were sent to the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region of Banja Luka, the leadership of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and the 1st Krajina Corps. This is a document that makes a series of demands and states a series of positions, and I'm going to identify two of those positions. In point 4, Mr. Pasic, the political representatives of the municipalities I identified demanded that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, particularly General Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats. And if we turn to item number 6 in that report, I'll read this in toto: "All seven municipalities in our sub-region agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of the municipalities. In this request -- respect, we request that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina provide a corridor for the resettlement of Muslims and Croats to Central Bosnia and Alija's independent state of BH because they voted for it. If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." This is a demand that is made in order to permit the Serbian authority to be maintained and implemented in your municipality, among others, Mr. Pasic. Did you attend this meeting where this particular -- these particular conclusions were reached?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really it's very difficult for me to remember whether I attended this meeting or not. I remember having been at some meetings in Sanski Most. Whether this particular one was one of them, I really can't remember at this moment. I know that I was not at the previous meeting that we spoke about. There were some meetings in Sanski Most but at this moment I really can't remember what kind of meetings those were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well if we turn to the next exhibit, Mr. Pasic -- the next tab, tab 19, I want to see if this might refresh your recollection, Mr. Pasic. Tab 19, Your Honours and Mr. Pasic, is an excerpt from a book -- the book is "It Is a Crime to Forget a Crime! Sanski Most in the War (1992 - 1995)." The two authors are Zilhad Kljucanin and Hazim Akmadzic, and I have excerpted a portion of this book. Your Honours will notice in the B/C/S version there is -- page 96 has not been translated. I noticed that last night. But Mr. Pasic, if you look at this text, you will see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need it or could we take it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should be taken out, page 96 should be taken out. I noticed it wasn't translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it an exhibit number already?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1031, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that starts with page 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It should start with 95, Your Honour, and then there is a 96, which is the page that is not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. It starts page 95 and then goes to 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, if you turn to page 99 in the B/C/S, this book cites the following people as having been present at the meeting of these subregional municipality heads that met on the 7th of June. It says, and I'll read them to you and perhaps this refreshes your recollection: Nedeljko Rasula, Nedeljko Anicic, Bogdan Latinovic, Dragan Ivanic, Simo Cisiovic, Milan Vojinovic, Gojko Kliskovic [phoen], Mladen Lukic, Rajko Novakovic, Radomir Pasic, Milan Kurjacic [phoen], Simo Drljaca, Mile Damjanovic, Bosko Marjanovic, Nikola Kokan, Simo Kurnjacic [phoen], Milan Kovacevic, Grujo Boric, Milomir Stabic, and Vlado Vrkes. Does that help refresh your recollection, Mr. Pasic, as to whether you attended the meeting in Sanski Most of the political representatives from the municipalities that are identified in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I did attend some meetings in Sanski Most. I don't know whether one of them is this particular one that you're talking about. I really can't say. I can't remember. I repeat, there were meetings in Sanski Most that I attended. Whether this meeting is one of them or not, I really can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's focus on item number 6, then, Mr. Pasic, because item number 6 is essentially a request coupled with a threat. The request to the leaders of the ARK is to provide a corridor for the resettlement of Muslims and Croats to Central Bosnia, and if the ARK leaders don't solve the issue, then all seven municipalities threaten to take all Muslims and Croats under military escorts from their respective municipalities. Did you participate in that meeting where that threat was made? Yes or no. I know you attended some meetings in Sanski Most. Did you participate in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I did attend some meetings. As for the types of threats that you have just spoken about, I'm really not aware of them and I can't remember whether within that context anybody spoke about Muslims moving out of Bosanski Novi, or Novi Grad as it was known at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you didn't attend this meeting, who was the political representative from your municipality who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me something that I really don't know. I'm saying that I cannot remember. It was a long time ago. It was very difficult for me to remember what happened each day or each moment. I repeat, I did attend some meetings. Whether I attended this one or some others, I really don't know. I can't even remember word for word what conclusions were made. Some conclusions were passed subsequently by a work group that I wasn't a member of. I repeat, this is something that I cannot either claim or deny, that something happened or did not happen. I simply cannot remember. My memory doesn't serve me that well. It's very difficult for me to say whether I attended a meeting of this sort. As far as I can remember, those people who went to those meetings from Novi Grad besides me, nobody asked for the forcible resettlement of population from Novi Grad. Solutions were sought as to how to help these people, how to overcome such a situation. That was the context. And all the meetings called for a solution to be found as to how to resolve the situation in Novi Grad. Our proposal was that there should be a peaceful way, without casualties, that people who wanted to leave should be provided with the means to go, that there should be some understanding for their requests. Last time I told you that this was our idea. If we had wanted to expel Muslims, we could have found easier options, but this was not our goal. This was not the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if we could turn now to the next tab, tab 20, this is a Prosecution Exhibit 529, Hanson tab 426. Mr. Pasic, this is a document -- do you recognise this document as bearing your signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not very legible. This is a very poor copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this document is dated the 8th of June and you have had a chance to cast your eye on substance of this. At the bottom there is a poorly reproduced signature, I agree with you. There is typewritten the name Radomir Pasic. This is an information --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask where the original is, or at least the copy from which this particular copy was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't have the answer at hand, Your Honour, but I'll find out and try to obtain the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the cross-examination on this point should stop until the witness sees the original, particularly bearing in mind the illegible passages in translation. That's my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Our submission, Your Honour, is that the substance of the document is clear and that the witness should be able, may be able to, in reviewing the document itself, identify and recall the document as something that he issued, even though he can't see the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber allows Mr. Harmon to ask the witness whether he has any recollection of ever having issued a decision with such a content, apart from whether he recognises this as his signature at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please provide me with a better copy? I can't see many of the words here. I would first have to read the text properly and then I will be able to tell you whether I did something or not. If you have a better copy, could you please give it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a copy here. I don't know if it's better than the one in front of the witness but I will read from the translation and it should be able to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to take the point again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The problem with the translation is there are significant important illegible passages that might be alleviated by a better copy being provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, if there is a better copy, then it would be preferable to have that one. At the same time, while translating the document, it seems that the interpreters were able to read -- well, most of it. And from what I learn from the translation, it gives sufficient context for a witness to remember whether he ever issued such a decision even if he would not remember each and every word of it. Mr. Pasic, would you try to do your utmost best to read from the document as good as you can, even if not every word would be readable, legible, would you please try to familiarise yourself with that portion of the document, which should be most of it, which is legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity, Mr. Pasic, to read the text that I have put in front of you? I will read -- if you can't read it well, I will read into the record a portion of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I assumed Your Honour was asking him to read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not ask the witness to do that, but I think most of the -- I can imagine that the Prosecution might be mainly interested in the last two paragraphs of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which are not the worst legible portions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the second paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I can read what has been translated for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, let me just orient you on this document so I can try to assist you and expedite this. This is a document that is issued from the Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff on the 8th of June 1992, addressed to the citizens of Blagaj and Japra valley. The subject is an information. And I will read this to you because I think it might expedite this. Parts of it are illegible, as you have said, but those parts that are legible I will read. "On 7 June 1992, you were informed by the Bosanski Novi Red Cross organisation about the problems of departure of Muslims from the territory of Bosanski Novi municipality. In the last three days, there have been war operations in the woods near Blagaj with the objective of eliminating the existing Muslim terrorist groups." And then there is missing text. "As members of the Serbian army are engaged on these tasks around the clock -" then it's illegible - "Serbian families at risk, there is a real danger for -" and then it is illegible - "population in Blagaj." Next paragraph: "Departure through Croatia and Slovenia organised by UNPROFOR was attempted before without success. The passage toward Banja Luka remains free. We hereby advise the citizens that we are prepared to provide a peaceful and secure departure of Muslim population from that area. With a view to your security, it is necessary to form a departure column immediately. The Crisis Staff and the Red Cross are prepared to assist with vehicles, food, and other needs. If these proposals are rejected, the Crisis Staff will no longer be able to guarantee security for Muslims in this area. President of the Crisis Staff Radomir Pasic," and then there is a signature. Do you recall having issued this document, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the Crisis Staff -- I was its president but I did not make decisions independently on my own. It was the Crisis Staff who made the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you've issued this document. No one asked you whether you took a decision alone or not. First question is: Is this a decision, taken by whomever, whatever form, was issued by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't remember. If this is your question and if you want a brief answer, I can only say that I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in the process of attempting to get the original document that we have and if it comes to me during this examination period, I'll present it to the witness and perhaps he can recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, on the 8th of June, in fact, when this particular information was issued, the military situation in Bosanski Novi was fully under military control. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not completely under the control of the army. I told you last time that we had a lot of problems with those paramilitary formations and we did everything we possibly could to avoid bloodshed and any knee-jerk actions. I've told you already that we could not have 100 per cent control in order to provide security and that we had a lot of problems with the paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next exhibit is found in tab 21. It needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 21, Your Honours will be P1032, and that will be for the regular combat report dated 9 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not going to show the witness this particular document. I'm going to direct Your Honours' attention to three paragraphs in this document and as well as the next document. This document, Your Honour, P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you treat it as a contextual exhibit and read it so that if the witness would have any comment on it, that he has an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be glad to do that, Your Honour. This is P1032.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, just for your information, it's also in tab, as I said, tab 21. This is a military secret 1st Krajina Corps command report, dated the 9th of June. It's a regular combat report directed to the Serbian Republic of BH Army Main Staff, and it is signed by General Talic. In the subpart 1, it says, about two-thirds down in the English: "The members of 'Green Berets' that were fragmented into smaller groups were attempting to pull out of the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Bosanski Novi, and move into Cazinska Krajina." If we go down to part 2, under Combat Readiness, mid-paragraph, it says: "Mopping up operations and the pursuit of groups attempting to break through to Cazin Krajina are continuing in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Bosanski Novi." And, 3, under Situation on the Ground, it says: "The situation on the territory within the zone of responsibility and the combat operations zone is under control." If we turn to subpart 8 in this document, on page 2 in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to take the greatest objection to this. If my learned friend wants to call evidence in rebuttal, then the Rules provide for that. The Court has already said that contextual documents the Prosecution want to put in at this particular juncture must be done with caution. We must be given a chance to comment and make submissions in relation to them. If the Prosecution are going to put in document after document, ask the -- if the witness is lucky, ask one question about whether his name appears upon it, that's one thing, and I've been told I can't object to that, but this is quite another course of action that my learned friend is now adopting, and I think it needs to be properly aired and properly argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Harmon wants to use this document in order to verify the correctness of the last answer of the witness, who said that there was no full military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the proper way of doing it is that Mr. Pasic will have an opportunity to read the document, that his attention is drawn to those portions of this document on which Mr. Harmon thinks that the last answer of the witness is contradicted, to see whether there is any -- whether it changes his mind or whether it gives rise to any comment. Therefore, it seems proper to me to draw the specific attention of the witness to certain portions so that he doesn't have to read all kind of irrelevant stuff, and at the same time it goes too quick for the witness to do it this way. So therefore, Mr. Harmon, you have asked the attention of the witness to the last portion of first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To the mid-paragraph -- subpart 2 of the mid-paragraph, dealing with mopping up operations. The first sentence in subpart 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please provide the witness with one copy of this document, indicating in the margin which specific, and then leave it until after the break to give an opportunity to the witness to comment on this document, in light of the last answer he gave. And if you have similar documents -- Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst that is being done, could I ask my learned friend's assistance, if he could try and attempt to obtain the original of P1030, because I want to re-examine and I think the Court will require the original, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The document we were handed this morning for the first time. The 14th of June 1992, Inter-Municipal agreements document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, could you assist Mr. Josse in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just marking for the witness those portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I do understand. A lot of work at the same time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could have the assistance of the usher, I could pass this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we leave that to the first break so the witness has a little bit more time to look at it, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I direct Your Honours' attention to that. I have another document that I would like to also direct Your Honours' attention to. I will mark the passages, and after the recess the witness can begin to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next document, Your Honour, is found at tab 22. And, Your Honours, I will mark this for the witness as well, but this also is dated the 10th of June. This is a 1st Krajina Corps command report, directed to the Serbian Republic of BH Army Main Staff, signed by General Talic, and I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to four portions of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might even consider to have an early break, Mr. Harmon, if you have identified the portions. Is it all about military control and presence of paramilitaries or Green Berets or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, this portion deals with the evidence that at this point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- according to these reports, the situation was under military control, and there are reflections of that in two secret military reports issued by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, the Chamber is considering whether it would be more appropriate to have a short -- a break now and give an opportunity to the witness but, of course, if you would have similar type of questions later on, then it might perhaps be better to wait and see what material is there to be read over the break and to see how much time the witness would need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make one brief logistical comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am anxious, when Mr. Pasic has finished his evidence, to then have a short break in any event. As a courtesy to him, as I am encouraged to do by the VWS, I would like to speak to him briefly. I would also like to speak briefly again to the next witness. I promised him I would do that immediately before he gives evidence. Just if the Court could schedule that. I would need about 20 minutes at that point in time, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Harmon, would a similar exercise, that is going through portions of documents and commenting on them in light of the answers given, would that be something that we could expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can expect it in at least two documents, Your Honour. Two other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two other documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So let's then continue at this moment. You may proceed and the witness will at least have a look at tab 21 and 22 but perhaps also to other tabs during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can direct Your Honours' attention to tab 22 -- which this also needs an exhibit number, I should say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1033, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In this particular document, Your Honours, I direct Your Honours' attention to subpart 1. Four lines from the bottom of that paragraph: "Groups of Green Berets attempting to withdraw to the Cazin Krajina are still present in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Bosanski Novi."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Subpart 2, starting at the third line: "In the areas of Prijedor, Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi municipalities, mopping up, catching and smashing enemy groups attempting to break through into the Cazin Krajina continues." Subpart 3, the first sentence: "The overall situation in the zone of responsibility and the combat operations zone is under the control of our forces." And subpart 8, second sentence: "Total control of the territory has been achieved, and mopping up of the area and disarming paramilitary formations continue fairly successfully."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You highlighted those portions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, that is the assessment of the military that was operating in your municipality at the time. Do you agree with that assessment or do you disagree with that assessment of the military, of General Talic and the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic had an office in Banja Luka, 100 kilometres from Novi Grad, and I very often disagreed with military assessments, at least when it came to the situation on the ground and safety and security on the ground, and so I don't agree with this information of Mr. Talic either. Now if he wrote that and said that, of course. I should like to repeat, the situation on the ground was as I had described it, and you could not have effective control at all times. That was impossible because of the paramilitaries. Now, whether Mr. Talic wanted to score some political points by writing things of this kind, I really don't know. That's not my field of expertise and I could not participate in talks of this kind or assessments of this kind. I'm -- it's not up to me to make an assessment or evaluation. I'm not competent enough to do that. But I'm speaking about what I myself experienced, what I lived through, and what I remember, how it was and what the situation was like. So I can't tell you anything else nor can I make an assessment of whether it is an objective assessment or subjective assessment of the corps or Mr. Talic, I can't say, but I personally consider that what you've just read out to me is an arbitrary assessment and that he very often wrote something that did not exist on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, returning back to the documents in tab 20, which is the information to the citizens of Blagaj and Japra valley, it describes war operations in the woods near Blagaj and says essentially that in order to secure the Muslims, for their security, they should depart. My question to you, Mr. Pasic, is: In light of these war operations that were taking place in the woods, in the Japra valley, what measures were taken by you or by the Territorial Defence or the army to secure the Serb villages from harm?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security tasks are something that I've already told you about, and that came under the Territorial Defence and the police station, the public security station, as far as they were able. It was impossible, in view of the given situation and the situation throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Novi Grad municipality itself, it was impossible to provide guarantees to anyone, either to the Muslims or the Serb population because the situation was one of chaos, when you really didn't know or couldn't know whether somebody's life would be at stake or jeopardised or not. So that part of the security situation that you've just asked me, I really can't say. We could not guarantee safety and security. Nothing was safe and secure, especially the way you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, why don't you answer the question? The question was what measures you took. Mr. Harmon confronts you with a situation, as suggested by this yet unverified document, that measures were taken to protect the inhabitants of Muslim villages by saying it's safer for you to move out, whether you took similar measures in respect of Serb villages in that same area. That's the question. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I understood it, you asked me about the security of the Serb villages. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what measures you took to protect. Let me just -- Mr. Harmon asked you, in light of these war operations that were taking place in the woods in the Japra valley, what measures were taken by you or by the Territorial Defence or the army to secure the Serb villages from harm in relation to the measures -- that's how I understood the question and that's the context of the question. In relation to the measures taken in respect of Muslim villages, whether you took similar or different or what measures you took in respect of Serb villages in order to protect or secure the population of those villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember any special measures being taken in that context. What I do know is that the Territorial Defence staff and the police -- I mean the public security station, that they worked, if I can put it this way, to further their tasks. And that was the goal; in some way to have those two organisations attempt to establish law and order, both in the Muslim part of the territory and the Serb part of the territory. I can't remember that any special measures were taken when it came to the Serb territories and the area populated by Serbs with any additional or special separate measures. I don't know that there was anything special or particular in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it you agree with me that none of the Serb villagers who lived in the Japra valley were asked to leave their villages and go to a specific location where they could be kept in a secure environment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You would have to know the configuration of the terrain, the Japra valley. You would have to know the places that the Serbs lived and the percentage of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Pasic, was: Were the Serb villagers in the Japra valley asked to leave their villages and go to another location where they would be more secure? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with a yes or a no because there was displacement from Serb houses as well, but not pursuant to a command. It was their own free will sometimes, their feeling for security. So there were instances like that where the Serbs left their houses too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, again, the question was not whether any Serbian families would have left their homes but whether they were asked to leave their villages and go to another location. That was the question. Did you ever make an announcement: "Please leave your homes, Serbian villagers"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that as far as I know, that didn't happen, but people did leave their houses for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is simply no such a -- this was not asked. Then, of course, you could have added whatever you wanted, but that's the answer to the question, it was not asked to them, and then you can add to that whatever you think is relevant. I now understand your testimony to be it was never asked, but that some from their own free will left their homes. And I'm now talking about Serbian families. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid you didn't understand me properly. You interrupt me quite frequently so I really cannot say and describe the actual situation, so I'm afraid that sometimes something will be omitted which would be very important for this Court to have the real truth and the proper information. So, please, you must understand me that it's impossible to answer certain questions with just a yes or a no and I consider that we can't discuss the matter in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the only thing I did is to urge you to first answer the question and then to add what you consider to be relevant in that context and not to tell us everything you consider relevant without answering the question. The question quite simply was whether you ever asked -- whether the Serbian families were ever asked to leave their homes. I now understand that they were not asked to do so, but that some of them did leave their homes. If this is an incorrect understanding of your testimony, please correct me. If it is a correct understanding and you think that there is any need to complete your answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I must say not in that type of context, but there were various pieces of information over the local radio, both for the Serb population and the Muslim population alike, to refrain from all types of military or similar voluntary, arbitrary operations and where they consider there was the risk to take shelter. So a general appeal was made to a possible security situation and that they should assess this themselves, but we said that we can't guarantee - I or the Crisis Staff or any of the authorities from the municipality - couldn't provide guarantees either to the Muslims or Serbs, so in that context, let me repeat, this did not refer, generally speaking, to the Muslims as a whole and the Serbs as a whole, but there was a general information sent out to the population of Bosanski Novi and Novi Grad. That means that we didn't target Muslims or target Serbs separately. We just issued warnings and tried to caution them and warn them of the situation we were in, and we tried to calm the situation down, and where it was felt that there might be an escalation in the conflict, that those sides should separate from each other. This referred to both the Muslims and the Serbs, and these were appeals which were very often made over the radio. Of course, there wasn't any electricity at that point in time, so the radio wasn't always working, but there were things of this kind going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, let's turn to the events that took place the day after this information was issued. And I'm referring to the removal of a large number of Muslims on train cars that took place in your municipality. I believe that is referred to in D115 of your report at page 10 in the English, and I'll read it. It says: "As the tensions and pressures from the populace in the area steadily grew, there was not a slightest possibility of any guarantees for them, so that appropriate measures were taken to allow the people to move out in the direction of Banja Luka, which was done on 8 June." Now that reference in this report of the work of the Crisis Staff, D115, refers to the removal of Muslims on the train cars, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it talks about the manner and reasons for which that population moved out, and I think we discussed that matter and expounded it earlier on, why this happened and how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Pasic, this reference to appropriate measures being taken refers to the removal of the Muslim population on the trains, and you answered the question, "Yes." Now, let me inform you, Mr. Pasic, that this Trial Chamber has heard considerable evidence of the circumstances under which that removal took place, including the murders of Muslims that took place at the location where Muslims were forced on trains, including the murder, Mr. Pasic, of Mr. Sifet Barjaktarevic, your fellow negotiator. It heard evidence of intimidation, shots fired over their heads, thefts of personal property. It heard evidence of the facts that there was no food, water, toilet facilities, protective garments, medical care provided to those people who were forced onto those trains and forced out of your municipality. Mr. Pasic, were you aware of that, those circumstances having taken place when the Muslim citizens of Bosanski Novi were forced onto trains and removed from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information. That there were certain conflicts in the Japra valley, yes, there were, I don't challenge that, but they were forced onto trains, I don't know about that, because I wasn't there. So that's one of the reasons. And the other reason is the one that I was informed of by the TO staff, that those persons were not forced onto train cars and that that departure on the trains, that prior to that there were talks between Mr. Sifet Barjaktarevic and Hamzagic where they asked, because you weren't able to go via Croatia at that time, asked that they go to Central Bosnia, and they just accepted this departure to Central Bosnia because they were afraid or they were unwilling to accept it but they did because they thought they would be mobilised and have to take up arms and go to war. So that's the sole reason that they put to me and they said that they didn't agree to go to Central Bosnia because it was a better, more acceptable option to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I asked if you were aware of that and you answered my question. You earlier testified that you were not present when the Muslim citizens of your community were forced onto those train cars. Was anybody from the Crisis Staff present? And I have -- again referring to D115, let me refer to some members who may have been there by virtue of their posts. Mile Damjanovic, commander of the TD municipal staff. Dragomir Kutlija, head of the public security situation. Ljubisa Latinovic, humanitarian and health and security. Dragomir Drazic, procurement food and refugees. Were any of those persons present when the Muslims in your community were forced onto those trains?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the way you asked that question would lead me to say yes, but I can't say yes because you've said a series of things that I don't agree with and I consider are not true, not correct. So the Muslims, that means, during that period of time, were not forcibly displaced by the territorial staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, what Mr. Harmon would like to know, what the Chamber would like to know, is whether any of the members of the Crisis Staff were present when these people boarded the train.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but before that, he asked me a shorter question that I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Harmon repeats, saying forced, where you say they went voluntarily, as far as you know, so therefore it's of no use to repeat that difference of opinion again and again and again in the questions. What the Chamber therefore I said, not only Mr. Harmon, but the Chamber would like to know is whether and which of these members of the Crisis Staff were present when these people were - and please mind my word - were boarding the train.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll answer your question. I don't remember of these people -- well, what I know is, and the command of the Territorial Defence staff Damjanovic told me then that this operation -- I think it was a position of the Chief of Staff of TO and that his name was Radislav Sekulic, that he was in charge and that he was in command of those people in Blagaj when that happened. Now, as for the people that you read out, I really can't remember whether during the day -- well, or whether that operation lasted a day or a day and a half, I can't remember, whether they were really there, I really don't know. At this point in time, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did they report to you as to the circumstances of the boarding of the Muslims on the train? Did they tell you it was peaceful and there were no events, no violent events that occurred in respect of the Muslims? Is that the information you received?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received information, as I said a moment ago, from the command of the TO staff, Mr. Damjanovic, to the effect that the action, the operation was conducted in such a way that they were not forced, they were not -- those people were not forcibly taken into the train cars but that he couldn't tell me what was happening around Blagaj, the upper part of the village, whether there was any shooting or not. And he assumed, he even assumed that there might have been some groups or small groups or paramilitary formations, units, because it's not a small place, which he could not control. He wasn't able to control that whole area, so he was just speaking about the railway station and the situation at the railway station itself and the way in which the people boarded the cars. So he informed me about that, and he also informed me, as I've already told you, that Mr. Sekulic was in charge of that operation. I think he was the chief, or that was his position, his function, in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'm going to turn back to the document which is the information, which is P529, that is found in tab 20. In -- specifically, the document says, in the penultimate paragraph, dealing with the removal -- with the departure of the Muslim population, it says: "The Crisis Staff and the Red Cross are prepared to assist with vehicles, food and other needs." That was the assurance that was given in this particular document bearing a typewritten name Radomir Pasic. Mr. Pasic, what steps did you take to ensure that the people -- that the trains that were leaving the municipality with thousands of your Muslim citizens had food, had water, had medical resources, had toilet -- proper toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already spoken about that, but let me repeat. In some way, that was a decision, or whatever you would like to call it, of the Crisis Staff, that those people, that is to say the people who entered the cars, should be enabled as far as possible, up to Doboj, the minimum conditions. They said that they would get -- Doboj would be the first station, that they would get off there, and that would be a journey of three to four hours, and I think that the Red Cross had precisely that function, to provide minimal elementary conditions, I think, in the form of food, bread, water, essentials. But let me repeat, I don't know who was in charge of that part of the work, which people. I really can't remember which people in concrete terms had to see to this, but there was this agreement to provide a minimum when it came to food, up until the time they were supposed to cross over into territory which at that time was under the control of the Muslim army and the politicians there. Doboj. Which is about 150 kilometres, if you go by train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we didn't know that this would last longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this document says the Crisis Staff are prepared to assist with food and other needs. My question to you is: You were president of the Crisis Staff. What affirmative steps did you take at that time to ensure that the trains had food and other needs, basic needs, to meet the civilian -- for the civilian population that was leaving on train cars, on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you said that the document says that the Crisis Staff is prepared to -- what it actually says is, "The Crisis Staff and the Red Cross are prepared to assist with vehicles, food and other needs," without giving any specification who would be responsible for what. Let's make it quite simple: Did you, as president of the Crisis Staff, take any action as far as preparation -- as providing food is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, operatively speaking, it is difficult for you to ask me that because that part of the operative work and how far the bakeries were functioning at the time, well, someone was in charge to see to that technical part, to hand it over and so on. I don't remember at this point in time, I think it was someone from the Red Cross. Whether there was someone from the Crisis Staff as well I really can't say. I can't say how the dynamics of this operation evolved but I know that there was talk of some things like that being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was talk about providing bread. Could you tell us, the Red Cross, what Red Cross actually was it you're referring to; International Red Cross, local Red Cross, republican Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was under one, the local municipal Red Cross. Now whether anybody from the International Red Cross took part I really wouldn't hazard a guess because I don't remember. I know they took part in some operations but what specific ones I really can't remember. There is the International Red Cross, of course. It was in existence, but whether at that time, whether it participated I really don't remember, I don't know. I think that they meant the local part of the Red Cross first. At that time, there was no communication for us to be able to talk about some other Red Cross apart from the local Red Cross. I don't think there was any other branch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the local Red Cross at that time operated by a mixture of Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, or was it a mono-ethnic operation? At that date. I'm not talking about the month before, but for this specific operation. If you know, please tell us. If you don't know, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seem to feel there was somebody from the Muslims. I think there was a woman but I can't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand your testimony well if you say, according to your recollection, there was one person of Muslim ethnicity, being a woman of which you do not remember the name, involved in the operations of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About other needs -- no, one other question. The assistance as far as vehicles are concerned, do you remember whether the Crisis Staff took any action in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that period of time, as far as vehicles are concerned, I don't think that it undertook anything. Those people went by rail, by train. At that time communications were difficult. It was difficult to go anywhere in any other form of transport. There was no fuel and a lot of shortages generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who provided for the trains? I mean, there were trains waiting for these people to allow them to leave. Who prepared for the trains?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the trains belonged to the railways of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. I don't know which of those people, somebody probably talked to someone from the railway station. I assume someone from the Crisis Staff in charge of that part, that they had contacts with those people, and then they directed the train towards Blagaj when the people went on board. As I say, I don't remember who the person was or the people were but somebody from the railways company, and somebody, I assume, from the Crisis Staff. I think that somebody might have talked to them to provide a train, because at that point in time that was the simplest and safest form of transport, to ensure that people leave the area that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You two times said you assumed. Of course, everyone could make assumptions in that respect. Is it that you don't know the name any more or that you do not know whether it was the Crisis Staff? What is the basis for your assumption, and what exactly is your assumption?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I really can't state for sure. Following on from the logics of the matter, it should have been someone from the Crisis Staff who discussed the matter. I know it wasn't me. Now, who it was I can't say, I can't claim, because I don't know for sure. I don't remember who it was exactly who talked to them, but I think it must have been someone at any rate from the Crisis Staff talking to the people from the railways to ensure that this train carry these people at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this the time, Your Honour, for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's time for a break as well. Mr. Pasic, you will be provided with the documents that were mentioned before. Those portions highlighted which, in the view of Mr. Harmon, need further comment or explanation in order to reconcile them with your answer about military control, would you please have a look at them during the break, and if there is anything you would like to add to the answers already given, because you explained to some extent already that you did not always agree and that you did not always know the specific reasons why matters were reported by General Talic as they were, if there is anything you would like to add, please do that then after the break. At the same time, Mr. Harmon, I think Mr. Josse is waiting -- was it the 14th of June? At least, the document with a clear name but not a clear signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 20 and also P1030, but I'll speak to my learned friend in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until five minutes past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, as far as the documents are concerned, do we have any progress to report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. The first document is the document that was found at tab 20. This is the information dated June the 8th. I have obtained a better copy, and it appears - and I'll present this to Mr. Pasic - it appears that someone signed on his behalf. I will present this document. I need it back, it can't be marked as an exhibit, but I will ensure that a better copy is provided at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at it then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- has seen it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can put it on the ELMO or I can pass it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the document, Mr. Pasic, the information dated June the 8th, and you will see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could he just have a look at it before it's put on the ELMO, please, and examine it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse would like to have look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He's seen it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honour. Could the witness look it. I've seen it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There appears, Your Honour, next to the name or word "za," which means "for" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are trying to get the picture of the ELMO, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As soon as the witness has finished examining it himself, it will be placed on the ELMO for Your Honours to see. Or I will pass it up to Your Honours. Let me pass it up to Your Honours after I ask a couple of questions of Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we could have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the document that is front of you is the document that's found in P20, and at the bottom it says your typed name, Radomir Pasic, it has the word "za," which means "for," on the left-hand side, and then there is a signature that is legible. Can you identify the signature, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please have it on the ELMO so that we can -- Mr. Pasic, would you please pass it to Madam Usher so that -- you're still able to look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It doesn't come out very clearly on the ELMO. Your Honour, may I pass it up to Your Honours and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that's the best idea because we are trying hard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you pass that document up to the Judges. They can examine the document. Okay. Madam Usher, if you could return it to the witness and after I've finished asking the witness one or two questions about that document if you could you return it to me, I will ensure the Court has a better copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, do you recognise the signature at the bottom, underneath your name, typewritten name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this is still a bad copy and I cannot recognise the signature. I can only assume -- I repeat, only assume -- that it is the signature from a member of the Crisis Staff, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you able to read the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could, then I would know who signed it. I really can't read it. This is still illegible, and this is what I've been trying to say, that sometimes documents were signed on my behalf, not by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When documents were signed on your behalf as the president of the Crisis Staff, were you given a copy of a document that was signed on your behalf, in the normal course of business?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The things were happening at such a speed that sometimes I did not even see a document. If something was not important, I didn't see it. If I considered something important, then obviously I had to see it, but there were some things that I didn't even see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The moving of the Muslim population from the village of Blagaj was something that was important. You've already established that in your evidence, Mr. Pasic. Is this a document you would have seen after someone signed it on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way people moved out was something important, something that I knew of, but not in operative sense. I'm not aware of how the operation was carried out. I know that they went by train, that's for the people of Blagaj, but I repeat, things happened on a daily basis, sometimes there were two or three conclusions in the course of one single day. So some things I didn't even see. Some things were done by other members of the Crisis Staff. Sometimes I would be absent from town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Pasic. Thank you very much. And if I could have that document, then, returned to me, I will, as I say, ensure that the Court gets a better copy of this. Mr. Pasic, then, given that we have taken a look at Defence Exhibit 115 and there is reference, at least two references on pages 9 and 10 of the English, dealing with discussions about the population in Blagaj and how to resolve that problem. Specifically, for example, on page 10, there is a reference, and we've discussed this before, the ARK government, the government of the Serb Republic of BH were asked to determine a decisive stand on the status of the Muslim population. It is clear from this report to the Crisis Staff that there was a dialogue between Crisis Staff representatives in your municipality with representatives at the highest levels, both in the ARK and in the republic level of the Serb leadership, that they were very much aware of the situation in your municipality. After the Muslims left your municipality on the trains, did you, did other members of the Crisis Staff, inform members of the leadership, the Bosnian Serb leadership, in Pale and in Sarajevo, about what had happened to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me a few questions. I will take your last question first. I don't remember whether we could have any contacts with the leadership of the Serbs in Pale. I don't know when they were informed, that is the official representatives of Republika Srpska, about the situation, but I don't think that it was immediately after the event. For technical reasons I believe this was not feasible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this document makes perfectly clear that you were able, members in your municipality, were able to discuss with the ARK government and the government of the Serb Republic the situation of the residents, the Muslims in Blagaj, because it's quoted in this report on the work of the Crisis Staff, so there were clearly communications with those higher echelons. So when you say there were essentially bad communications, Mr. Pasic, I submit that there were sufficient communications, as reflected in this document on this topic, with leaders in -- at those upper echelons. My question to you is, and I want you to try to think very clearly on this, when did you inform the leadership at the level of the Bosnian Serb Republic level about what had happened to the Muslims in Blagaj? And when I say "when did you," I'm referring to you personally or members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were communications, but the communication wasn't good, and I personally was affected by that. I really don't know when I or, rather, the Crisis Staff or somebody from the Crisis Staff informed the leadership in Pale. I believe that this information went to Banja Luka first, but, again, I don't know when that information was forwarded to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With whom was this information forwarded in Banja Luka? Who did you tell about the removal of the Muslims from your community in -- who did you tell in Banja Luka about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say I sent the information. I assume that somebody received the information, I don't know who. I don't know whether it was Kupresanin or somebody else. I wouldn't dare say anything specific at this moment. I don't remember that and I cannot claim that it was one of those people. Somebody was informed, but I really don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Somebody was informed. Do you know who informed that somebody? Did you personally or did somebody from the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just said that I really don't know when this happened, who did it. I suppose that somebody from the Crisis Staff sent the information about the situation. I repeat, it is impossible to take hold of all those details because those details changed by the day, even by the hour, and as to who went to whom, the information was given, it's very difficult to say with any degree of reliability at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it that your answer is the same if I were to ask you, Mr. Pasic, who at the republic level did you or members of the Crisis Staff inform about the removal of the Muslims from Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, we cannot talk about the removal of Muslims from Blagaj, and I already answered that I don't remember when they were informed. I believe that, as I've already told you, there was -- there were means of communications but there was not enough communication and this is something that I was personally affected by, the fact that there was not enough communication, and I believe that many people in high positions did not know the real information about what was going on. Even I didn't know about some things that were happening in the Japra valley. It was impossible to be aware of all those details at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, how far was your office from the rail head where the Muslims were placed on the train cars?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately ten or 11 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Pasic, as a result of the removal of Muslims on cattle cars, is it a fair statement to say that the majority of the Muslim population in Bosanski Novi municipality was no longer present?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question. Can you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll be glad to. As a result of the events that we have been talking about, the removal of Muslims on train cars from Bosanski Novi municipality, the majority of the Muslim population was removed. The majority of the Muslim population from your municipality was removed.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They were not removed, not a majority, not a minority. Those who left, I really don't have any reliable information, but if we are talking about the total number of Muslim population in the municipality of Novi Grad, then we are talking about a smaller number of people who left the municipality of Novi Grad during that period. I would like to say that there were some 14.000 to 14.500 Muslims residing in Novi Grad and only a small number of them left, maybe 2 or 3.000, approximately. I suppose that that's how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
