utterances.text: Now, let's focus on the approximately 750 men who were on those trains who were returned to Bosanski Novi. They were returned, I think, on the 11th of June 1992. You recall that, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the male population that were loaded onto those trains, returned. I don't know whether were 750 of them. I believe there were not as many. I can't say how many. I know that they returned from the direction of Doboj and that they arrived in Novi Grad, Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, that, Mr. Pasic, I am assuming that that was quite a surprise to you and to members of the Crisis Staff, and therefore my question to you, Mr. Pasic, is: Having received these men back into your municipality, who did you contact as to why they had been returned? When I say "you," Mr. Pasic, I'm referring to you and/or members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that this was news to us. This was not envisaged, we didn't know that this would happen. I believe that the information was received from the railway company. As the train travelled, the communication followed. Train stopped after Doboj in the direction of Maglaj, and there these people --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't need the details about what happened to the men. I asked you, Mr. Pasic, who, once the men returned to Bosanski Novi municipality, who in the leadership level of the ARK, and who in the leadership level of the republic government level, did you contact, if anyone, to discuss the return of those men?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just going to say that we were left to our own means and we had to come up with adequate solutions on our own. We were at a stalemate. It was a fait accompli. We didn't know what to do when these people returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, let me stop you again. Why not answer the question? Did you contact anyone at the higher level? Yes or no. You or one of the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think I did, and I don't remember that anybody from the Crisis Staff did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That fully answers the question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you testified, Mr. Pasic, that you personally never went to the stadium to see where the -- Mlakve stadium where these men ultimately were detained. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence in this case, Mr. Pasic, that there was insufficient food for those detainees at the stadium, there were no blankets, there were two toilets, there was no soap, no hot water, no medical care, there were random beatings of the Muslim detainees, there were humiliations. The Court has heard evidence in this case of those detainees signaling SOS signals to across the river into Croatia, to UNPROFOR troops, has heard the testimony of at least one witness who lost 20 kilograms during his stay in the Mlakve stadium. Mr. Pasic, what steps did you and members of the Crisis Staff, take to ensure the well-being of the Muslim men who were detained in the stadium? If you could just list the steps that you personally took or members of the Crisis Staff took.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask why that question required all the detail that is within it? The question could simply have been what steps were taken, et cetera. If my learned friend is going to have the detail, then he should put it to the witness and ask whether he can comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Harmon, you should first ask the witness whether he was aware of the situations. And then Mr. Josse, if I just may say one more word about this witness, if it's not explained in quite some detail to him what is meant with the question - so the word "well-being" might have been misunderstood about - it gives rise to a lot of other fields. And Mr. Harmon, by the examples, at least specified what kind of well-being he was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, were you aware of those circumstances as I described them, that applied -- that affected the Muslim detainees at the stadium? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the circumstances that you listed and I don't think that the circumstances were such. I've already said what treatment those people received and why they were at the stadium, so I wouldn't agree what you said in your question, that part of your question. I never received any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The second part of my question, Mr. Pasic, was what affirmative steps did you personally take or did members of the Crisis Staff take to ensure and to monitor the well-being of the men who were detained at the stadium? If you could just answer that specific question, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the well-being of these people, and for security reasons, they were placed in the stadium. They were not safe because of the paramilitary formations. Secondly, these people were treated in a humane way and the staff of the Territorial Defence was in charge of that. I don't know anything about the operative matters, but I was informed that they received food from the barracks where the troops were billeted and that they shared their food. They were even -- they were even allowed to receive food from their families, even some Serbs who had friends among those Muslims brought either food or clothes so to the stadium. This was allowed. The Mlakve stadium is in the direction of Krupa, and for objective reasons, they could not send SOS signals across the Una River because they would not have been visible. So somebody must have been -- misinformed you about all those things because they are just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The question I asked you was what affirmative steps did you personally take or did members of the Crisis Staff take to ensure and to monitor the well-being of the men who were detained at the stadium. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've answered your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the answer to the question --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can clarify, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the answer to the question to be that care was taken that everything humanely needed would be provided to those in the stadium but that you have no operational details to your knowledge. Is that correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it wasn't prepared in advance, if you're thinking of some preparation. There couldn't have been any preparation, as I said, because as far as we were concerned, this was a novelty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about preparations. First of all, I'm summarising your testimony. And I do understand that you have no personal knowledge of ordering bread to be sent there or clothes to be sent there or soap to be sent there; that you were informed that everything would be taken care of. Is that a correct understanding, without knowing any further details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's precisely what I wanted to say and what in fact I did say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time, Mr. Pasic, that the men were being detained at the Mlakve stadium, the entire zone of the 1st Krajina Corps, including Bosanski Novi, was under military control. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If, Your Honour, we could -- the next exhibit, if we could turn to tab 23, this is Prosecution Exhibit 193, I've highlighted the portion of this document during the recess and it has been shown to Mr. Pasic. So I will refer Your Honours to two passages in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, did you have an opportunity to read the relevant documents and especially the portions highlighted by Mr. Harmon? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, P193, is a 1st Krajina Corps command military secret, dated the 14th of June 1992, submitted to the Serbian Republic Army Main Staff, and it is signed by Major General Momir Talic. I direct Your Honours' attention to the first complete paragraph, five lines from the bottom of that paragraph, where it says: "The entire zone of responsibility is fully under control." And then, Your Honours, I would like to direct Your Honours -- well, actually, let me then ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness Pasic, do you disagree with Mr. -- with General Talic's assessment that he forwarded to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't agree. In the case of the Novi Grad municipality. I can't speak for the others. I'm not placed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in fact, these people who were kept in the stadium were not permitted to return to their villages. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I've already spoken about that matter. I said that for security reasons, they were placed there and that there was the danger of their lives being jeopardised by paramilitaries, so not the Territorial Defence staff but the small groups of people who were out of control, who couldn't be controlled because it was a large area, and we couldn't provide their security, and I've already said that five or ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you was they were not permitted to return to their villages, were they, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not so. That's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They were permitted to return to their villages, Mr. Pasic? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understood me. I told you the reasons why, when they came from Doboj, for what reasons they were put up in the stadium. So I repeat, it wasn't a question of permitting or not permitting people to go to their village, it was a case of a security situation and how far it was safe for the people to return to their houses and homes or to be in some other place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, a clear question for you: Who decided whether or not to take the risk to be subject to any violence of these paramilitary groups? Did you say, "Go home if you want, but please be aware that it's dangerous over there," or did you say, "For security reasons, we will not allow you to go home because it's too dangerous over there"? Which one of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't do either of those two things. The Crisis Staff, I think, together with the centre for public security, that is to say the police, and the TO staff, was faced with a situation that it had to take some decision, but what, they didn't know themselves. And a solution was sought, something that was most suitable and most acceptable, and which at that point in time would be the least painful. Now, I don't know who made the proposal but the proposal anyway was that it would be dangerous for these people to go back to their houses because they couldn't provide -- the TO couldn't provide any security or guarantees, nor was the police able to issue those guarantees, so it was for those reasons. So neither question was put the way you put it. The only question was how to provide security for these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if they wanted to go to their villages, would they be allowed or were they allowed to go there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have information because those people already wanted to go to Doboj. I didn't have information as to whether they wanted to go back to their own houses or not, and they didn't know whether they were going. This was something they couldn't foresee, just like we couldn't foresee it. So this is something that those people didn't know about at that time, nor did we know what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, whether they could foresee it, yes or no. Someone could have told them, they could have thought about certain risks. Now, please, a clear answer, unless you say, "I don't know," then of course you don't know. Were they allowed to go to their homes if they wanted to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said, I think, I don't know whether that question was asked of those people. I wasn't there. I wasn't present. I don't know if anybody asked them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know -- well, first of all, they could have asked those who were in charge of their safety, but what I do understand is that you do not know whether they ever asked to go home, whether they were ever offered an opportunity to go home; you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I do know is that the majority of those people, when they arrived from Doboj and were located at the stadium, that immediately, or two or three days later, that most of those people was released. But not to their houses. They were put up with their friends in town because there were some measure of safety and security there rather than in the villages where they lived, in the Japra valley. So most of the people were released to go and stay with family or friends and there were even some Serbs who provided security and safety for them and refuge for them in their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, let me direct your attention then to another paragraph that's found in P193. It's a paragraph which is -- Your Honours, on page 3, the paragraph directly above subpart 3 of the document. You've had a chance to see this, Mr. Pasic. Let me read this: "The most difficult situation concerns the Muslim and Croat refugees in the area of AR Krajina, their security and the provision of food. The attempt to expel them to Central Bosnia failed because of transportation difficulties and their resistance to leaving their places of residence." Mr. Pasic, the reason the Muslims were kept and detained in Mlakve stadium was in order to find a solution to their expulsion from your municipality. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The men who remained in the Mlakve stadium until the 23rd of July 1992, we are informed in this -- through evidence in this case, Mr. Pasic, were released only after they signed a document saying, one, they wouldn't return to Bosanski Novi, and two, they either exchanged their property or gave it -- or forfeited it to the municipality. Are you aware of that type of a document, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That type of document, as you've just presented to us, I don't know about. What I do know is that people sold or exchanged their property and solved their property status, but that they signed a piece of paper saying they wouldn't return, I don't know about that. Let me repeat, I think this was a subject of discussion where the Crisis Staff allowed people to move out voluntarily, and I think that the Crisis Staff, for those reasons, asked that they confirm this, that they were leaving of their own free will, as they had indeed asked to do, and that they should settle their property status. That is to say, what they weren't going to take with them, they should deal with. And so during the conflicts and after the conflicts, through the paramilitaries formations in the Japra valley, some of the property was destroyed, and the Crisis Staff considered -- we considered, the Crisis Staff considered -- that it was possible if they -- impossible if they moved out, it was impossible to safeguard their property, that the municipal authorities could safeguard their property. And so for that reason they were asked to deal with their property in some way if they wished to leave the area. So we couldn't give them guarantees that would be able to look after and save their property, but if they were able to find a solution to their property problems, whether by selling it or exchanging it, then the possibility was there to save their property until such time as they should return. So this form existed by which they solved their property status and property problems in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, on approximately the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This stadium, now we are going around and around on this matter. We have been going around and around for several minutes. I would like to know, where was this stadium? Was it out of the town or was it within the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was out of town, about three to four kilometres away from the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your own profession, your own occupation, was it in town, downtown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have found yourself close to this stadium? At any moment, have you been close to this stadium?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I went to work from the opposite direction, the opposite part of town, so I didn't have to pass by that part of town, and I've already emphasised that I didn't go to the stadium because that part of town, the -- or rather, the operative part was conducted by the TO staff and by the police. So mostly that part was under the Territorial Defence staff so that I myself really didn't, during that period of time, when the people were there, go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you didn't have a permission to do so? There was a permission needed to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know whether I needed any authorisation or permission to -- permission, to be quite frank, but let me repeat, in view of the problems that cropped up on a daily basis, there was a sort of division of work in that part of town so that I didn't feel the need, I myself, to appear there. I don't know how I could have contributed with my presence at the stadium, if I had appeared there myself. So I believed and trusted the people who did that part of the work, and let me repeat, it was the Territorial Defence staff that saw to that and all the operational matters; food, water, accommodation, and all the rest of it and the distribution thereof. So it wasn't my job and I didn't have to tour the stadium, and that it would have been impossible for me to go around all these segments and see to all these things. Either theoretically or practically, it wasn't feasible, for everything that was happening at that time, for me to see it personally as president of the Crisis Staff or experience it or take part in it. I think that was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely. So again the same question concerning the transfer of the Muslims by train. Could you see how -- how this train was formed, constituted? Where did it happen? Was it at the station, the railway station proper? The convoy started from where? Where did the train start from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already stated that I wasn't present, that the train left from the Blagaj station, which is approximately ten or 11 kilometres away from the centre, roughly - you can measure the distance, of course - but it was the Blagaj, and that's where those people boarded the [inaudible], and it was the Territorial Defence staff that was in charge of that part of the operation. I think it was a man in fact by the name of Radoslav Sekulic, and I think his post was Chief of Staff of the TO. He was the operative man there, but let me repeat again I myself wasn't present, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if you had had the curiosity or the wish or the will to see how things were going on, would it have been possible for you to go and see how the train, the convoy was constituted, and which way -- how things were going on? Did you have physically the possibility to go and see how things were going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think physically in one way or another it wasn't safe or secure to go because, as I say, there were things happening every day and any journey was a risk. You put your life at risk. So that I would have been exposed to the same situation even if I had wanted to go. I would have run a danger in going from any side. Yes, there was the danger because there was a war on, after all, and the regular units bore weapons and certain small paramilitary groups would intercept cars on the roads, and Serbs on the roads even, and there was this great risk of travelling anywhere at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you consider that these Muslim families and these Muslims, as your co-citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I considered them to be my own citizens regardless of their ethnicity. This wasn't a situation that I had prepared or I had the power of decision-making, and you couldn't control certain things. So, of course, quite normally we were faced in the situation when we were brought into danger ourselves. In the centre of town we were endangered, where the Crisis Staff was located and the municipality building was located, so there were situations like that too. But let me repeat, you couldn't control everything, nor could you tour all these sectors of town and be on the spot in different localities, so I wasn't there myself and I wasn't present during that event either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would simply like to know, Mr. Pasic, you had responsibilities in those days, administrative responsibilities, political responsibilities, which were important. Your co-citizens, and I'm now speaking of the Muslims, and you do call them that way, your co-citizens, were in a situation which was extremely difficult and probably twice; when there was this departure by convoy, by train, and later for others in this stadium. Don't you think, may a judge wonder about the fact that you did not, because you had certain powers, that you didn't take a decision or make a decision to gather people from the military or people from the TO who could have protected you and in the case you would have wanted to see on the spot what was going on? Couldn't it be a bit strange, a bit surprising, when you have 700 people who are kept within a stadium, when you've got several thousand people who are put on a train and those are your co-citizens and you have responsibilities, may I be surprised that you haven't done everything you could to go and check and control what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you couldn't say that, if I followed your question correctly, that I was quite indolent towards any of this, but let me repeat I had no special authorisation, nor special tasks, and quite simply physically it was impossible for me, as the president of the Crisis Staff, to tour the whole terrain. That's one point. The second point is this: I wasn't alone in the municipality. There were other very important and shall I say key functions of these people, such as the TO staff and headquarters, the police. So these were operative things where the chief of police should appear first, the commander of the TO, and some other persons of that format - the civilian police, for example, or the army - to create law and order. That's what we asked them to do and that's the task that they did do. So that it wasn't up to me at that point in time, if I may say so. I don't know what I would do now, but let me repeat, I was not either at the stadium or the village of Blagaj because I considered that it would be the people whose operative job it was to do that, that they would do that better than I could ever do, so my presence would not have contributed to anything. I would just have been a passive observer, I wouldn't have been able to contribute anything, and that's why I thought it was superfluous for me to appear there as some sort of passive observer. I might have been subjective in a situation like that and I don't know what decision I would have made or could have made because I said at the beginning that I don't understand strategic military matters. I'm not well versed in matters concerning the army. I was just a regular soldier in the army. So certain things in that part of town, when it came to operative matters, the police, the army, I really wasn't -- I didn't interfere in things like that now did I have the need to meddle in anything like that. So let me repeat, they were just operational matters that somebody had to do pursuant to their post and position, such as members of the Crisis Staff, and members of the Crisis Staff or also people from the police or from the Territorial Defence. So it is for these reasons that I did not appear there, I didn't go there because I considered it would be these people who would do their -- this job quite naturally in the normal course of their jobs, and you had to trust and have confidence in some people. If you distrusted everything, then we could have done nothing in difficult situations of that kind. So for many reasons there was no need for me to visit these places and localities. How shall I explain this to you? Well, let me say that I can't say I wasn't worried by the problem, that it didn't concern me in a way and that I didn't feel it emotionally. Of course it did. Of course it was a difficult situation. Of course it was difficult to explain now, let alone live through it and experience it in that year of 1991, but let repeat, some things were impossible to do. You couldn't influence certain things and you couldn't go and see all these things personally and take part personally and make decisions personally or make conclusions personally in every given situation. It was a great problem, that is true, but let me repeat - and this is something that I said last time - in talking to the representatives of the Muslim population, in a way I was in the civilian portion and I sought solutions there, to do as much as possible for those people so that they could in a painless way, in a voluntary way, according to their request, should be allowed to leave, and it was really their goal not to go to Central Bosnia, and I've already said that and I don't want to repeat the reasons for that, their object was Croatia. They wanted to go to Croatia and central Europe because mostly they had friends and relatives already living and working there in one way or another as guest workers, as we call them. So let me repeat: I was focusing on this civilian part of the job rather than the exclusively operative military part of the job. So perhaps that's the reason. Now 13 years later, I don't want to seek any justification for what happened, I'm just telling you what did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So when you specify that you were keeping to your civil responsibilities in general climate, which is the one you've just described, in which sector do you consider you should have limited any form of intervention from your part, as president or chairman of the Crisis Staff? In which field or domain did you think you had to act? What was -- if you had nothing to do with the security or safety of your co-citizens and the way things were going on for the Muslim part of the population, of your population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood the question correctly, first let me say that I consider -- or you consider that I had some far-ranging authorisation, which I didn't have. I didn't have any special authorisation or competence. Unfortunately, I was not given those by anyone. I didn't have them. And I wasn't able, I myself, to decide one way or another on certain matters and make a decision myself. So it wasn't a question of my own subjective or objective assessments. I couldn't have been in that situation. I was never able, I myself, as Radomir Pasic, to make a decision or conclusion without that question having been considered by other members of the Crisis Staff to find an adequate solution. We considered ourselves to be a team. It was team work. Or let us call it a body, an organ which was there to find solutions, and amongst ourselves we divided up the jobs, who was in charge of what, doing what. So it was for these reasons that that is what happened. Quite simply certain -- some people never appeared, just I happened to appear for certain negotiations, but similarly I didn't appear when some other matters were discussed or when some other things were taking place. So there was this division in the Crisis Staff. I was just the presiding officer of the Crisis Staff, and I wasn't able to decide one way or another, if I liked something or didn't like something. And sometimes on many matters I might not have agreed, but if that it was the position taken by the majority, then of course I had to abide by that decision and adopt the positions of the majority and the conclusions they had made. I don't mean any essential issues but certain operative matters. There might have been a number of ways in which something could have been done and solved and I might not have agreed but it was the position taken by the majority and I had to accept that. So I myself did not have any special authorisations. I was a member of the municipal assembly as president of the Crisis Staff, but as I say, my remit was not above anybody else's authorisation or competence, nor did I have any greater powers or force, political powers or anything else. If anybody thinks I did, I really didn't. So I wasn't able to make decisions, arbitrary or otherwise. Things like that just didn't happen that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I would have a few questions for the witness. Mr. Pasic, I have some questions. The questions are quite short. I would like to receive short answers as well. Did you ever visit the stadium prior to or after the events, even after the war, the stadium we talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was at the stadium before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the layout of that stadium is concerned, is there a gallery for the spectators or for the public at all sides of the stadium, or at one or two or three or four, so a built-up constructed gallery for the spectators? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On one side, there are stands facing the Una River, the part of Croatia, and there is also a fence made of cypresses that are a few metres high on the other side. So it's a hedge, a cypress hedge, opposite the stands. And this is on the eastern part of the stadium, in the direction of Vidorija and Javlaca [phoen]. This is the inner part of the city. This part is visible. It's open. It is visible from one part of the town and it is not visible from the direction of another part of the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I just asked you at how many sides of the stadium there was a gallery for the public. I do understand that it was on one side. It was on one of the long sides of the -- of the football ground, as usual in stadiums? Yes, and did I hear you say that it was on the western side of the football ground, of the play ground itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say it was north-west. It was more to the west but one part of it was also to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that -- you talked about the Una River. What's the distance between the stadium and the Una River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Una River is close, maybe 40 or 50 metres away from the stadium. Maybe not even that far. The river bends here. It doesn't flow in a straight line, it makes a bend exactly at that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us about this fence, a few metres high. What should I think of, a few metres? Three metres, four metres, two metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to the stands, there was also a hedge, a cypress hedge, which were a couple of metres high and very dense, so one couldn't see through the -- this is what I was saying, so this hedge was rather thick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And at what side exactly was this hedge or this fence? Was this opposite side of the spectators' gallery or same side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on one of the sides to the north, as you are looking towards one part of Novi Grad. I believe that this hedge was to the north as you look from that part of the town, and as when you're looking from the stands, then it is north-west. The hedge also curves a little and one part of it is on the opposite side as well, but that opposite side is not as long as the main part of the hedge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could this sketch be put on the ELMO. Madam Usher, could you please assist me. Madam Usher, could you please zoom out in such a way that the whole of the sketch is visible. Or is that impossible? I think we -- I made a sketch, Mr. Pasic, of what seems to be a football ground. I also made the sketch on the spectator gallery being on one long side of the football ground. Could you indicate to me where we find the Una River, even if you would like to -- is it to the right? Is it up? Is it down? Is it to the left? Could you tell us where the Una River is at a distance of some 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you'll allow me, I could draw it on this paper, if you will allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would allow you to do that. Have you got a pen there? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Una would make a bend here. This is the direction of its flow. This is the Una River. Here there is an auxiliary stadium. This is where the Una is closer to the stadium. These are the stands, if I understand the word well, and this is a semi-circle behind the stands. Maybe this is not a good scale. The distance is somewhat bigger here, but this is where the hedge is, also in a semi-circle. This is the cypress hedge which is a couple of metres high. And if you're looking in this direction, this is Novi Grad, and this part here, I believe this is the southern part of the stadium, this is the north-western part, and this should be the eastern part of the stadium. This here is the road leading to Bosanska Krupa in this direction, and approximately here, this is where the main entrance to the stadium was, and this is where the stadium was open, and here you see the hedge which fenced the stadium off. And I repeat that this is where the area was the highest. I believe that the stands are some 15 to 20 metres high, according to my estimate, and this part was closed off or fenced off, and I don't think that it should be -- could have been seen from anywhere - maybe from a plane - and this part here could be seen from the road, and here, this part was slightly turned to face south-east. You couldn't see anything from the houses, because there are some houses here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I said that I would put short questions to you. Let me take over and take you to the matters I found most -- find most relevant. Could you please move the sketch a tiny little bit down so that we see the upper part of it. Could you tell me how the river Una continues. Because it stops halfway the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, it bends here and makes another semi-circle and starts flowing in a straight line in this direction. The Bosnian side is somewhat narrower and this is where it widens up. There are some fields here. But down there, it is a bit narrower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I take it that all on the right side of the stadium, that's all Bosnian or Republika Srpska territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is Republika Srpska, and this is Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the Croatian side, are there any hills or is it hilly, or is it all flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bank along the Una is flat. I don't know how far it is flat, but I would say that it is more flat on the other side than it is on this side. That area over there, across the river, is flatter. There are some hills over there but they are not very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could they establish a line of sight between the stadium and these hills?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look from here, it is impossible. It is impossible to see anything because of the stands, which are rather high. So if you're looking from here, in that direction, you can't see anything but the stands and the sky above them. The line of vision is non-existing here, and if you tried to see the ground, you couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in the direction I called up, would there have been a line of sight to the hills on the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to this part here? Is this what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about if you would draw a line approximately - I'm not inviting you to do it - but parallel to the stand, just in the direction up there, it crosses the river a bit further up, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that again you can't see anything because there is a hedge here, and here, behind the goal, there is a large net so as to prevent the balls flying over the fence, and again the height is about some ten or 15 metres, so one could not go anywhere beyond the stadium in this direction because this is all fenced off, so to speak. This is a sports stadium, a football stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it still fenced up? Is the hedge still there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can still see it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P82. I took out some of what seems to be comment on the -- apart from what I would say the rather neutral ones. Could you please have a look at that. It will be put on the ELMO. Oh, it's -- no. It's supposed to -- yes, could you please cover the text that -- Mr. Pasic, the green spots at the end of the stand for the spectators, is that Croatian territory or is that Republika Srpska territory? Let's just be sure that there is no misunderstanding. That is the green spot above the head of the lady where, on the top of that hill, there seems to be a wooded area, is that Croatian or is that Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to this, I believe that this is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it seems that the river you made on the sketch has moved a bit, isn't it? Because this is a line which is not parallel to the stand but goes rather to the left of the line of sight, and if you take a similar line on your sketch, I end up in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not a geography graduate but if you had a map of Novi Grad, you could see it and dispel all your dilemmas. You would see the actual situation. Nothing can be moved. Nothing can be hidden. It is still visible today. And I believe that you can obtain the hundred per cent correct facts either from a map or if you go there and take photos. All this would provide you with the only correct picture of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you're perfectly right that on the basis of just a river put there on the spot by hand, that one could not draw any final conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, may I take it that detailed maps are available of this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll be glad to check, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the Chamber would like, in order to verify the conclusions drawn on the basis of a sketch which, of course, could not be binding to the extent that the exact position of the river would be remembered by the witness but I take it that the Una River has not changed its bed over recent years and usually football stadiums are well indicated on maps, and even directions are very often. So therefore the Chamber would very much like to receive such additional information. But, of course, if the Defence would have any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm looking, Your Honour, at a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we would really need a detailed map as --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll make an inquiry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My only observation is I'm all in favour of that, bearing in mind the exercise that the witness had been invited to carry out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I would not just rely on how he positioned the river but, of course, for the questions to be put to him, I invited him to do it and it may well be that it's not fully consistent with what we find on a map, so therefore it's worth to verify that on a good map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I'm looking at the clock. It's 12.30. It has been 12.30. In view of the time already taken in cross-examination, what -- as a matter of fact, there is no time left, as far as I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour is asking me how much time I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I said that -- I started asking you how much time you would still need and then I changed my question into an observation, which is that, as far as I'm aware of, that there is no time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Court to permit me to ask approximately 15 minutes more of questions. There are some important issues that I can cover very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, how much time would you need for re-examination, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Mr. Harmon you've got another ten minutes, we'll then have a break, and Mr. Josse you'll have the time remaining. Then we first have to give a number to my sketch, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be C-1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: C-1, and that's a sketch of a football ground, with additional markings made by the witness, Mr. Pasic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, on the 20th, approximately the 20th of June, 1992, you received a letter informing you that the mass transfer of population, mass -- the forced mass transfer of population on purely ethnic or racial basis has been declared a crime against humanity, and in fact, that wasn't the only time you received that information; is that correct? You can answer that question yes or no. And I'm referring Your Honours and Mr. Pasic to the exhibit in tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to be pedantic. He's not referring Mr. Pasic to it. The question is fair enough. If he wants to refer Mr. Pasic to the document, Mr. Pasic needs to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Pasic testified about this statement already, that he had received such a letter. I was trying to be -- assist the witness. Perhaps the witness can answer the question yes or no and I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first -- Mr. Harmon, you are -- you said approximately the 20th of June, and then you refer us to tab 24, which contains several documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The second document is a letter directed to Mr. Pasic, dated the 20th of June. I believe he's testified about that. And the first document in there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- 22nd of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a letter of the 20th of June, Mr. Pasic. Perhaps let's -- did you receive a letter at that moment with the content as just referred to by Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please jog my memory? I don't know what this is about. There have been a number of letters. I don't know what letter you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you turn to tab 24 in front of you, you'll see a copy of the translation of that letter in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the witness have the right -- it's 449, last three digits, I take it, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't believe the witness has the correct document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be put on the ELMO to start with. Its last three digits of the number at the top, at the right-hand side, is 449. And the letter starts at the second part of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can just make a copy. I can tear my copy out of my exhibit and just give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just pass this to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness, we direct your attention to what the usher is handing you. You'll see this is a letter addressed to you, and I direct your attention to the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on page 4 of the B/C/S. Have you found it, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking. I'm trying to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, did you receive a copy of this letter?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean then? At the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. There were a few of them, but I believe that this letter was one among those that reached me. I can't be sure of that. I spoke with Mr. Kirudja and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasic, the message that was expressed in that particular fifth paragraph is something that you had been informed of earlier in your previous contacts with international representatives. Is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want me to say is correct or not, what he wrote or what I replied. I really -- I'm aware of the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. The question was whether in your earlier contacts reference was made to the same issue that is the -- that the forced mass transfer of population on ethnic or racial basis has been declared a crime against humanity, whether that issue was raised in your previous contacts with your interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not this in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I direct your attention then in the same tab, the tab 123, to the letter dated the 22nd of June, and particularly the second paragraph. I won't go into it further at this point because I have limited time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I object. I'll deal with it another time but I take objection to that sort of comment in the course of evidence. This is cross-examination, not speech time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in the -- let me -- I want to spend one minute on this topic if I can't get the answer on this. Mr. Pasic, this document that I have referred to that is in the same tab says as follows: "Please find attached a letter addressed to the mayor of Bosanski Novi by the representative of an international organisation. This letter, particularly the fifth paragraph, is designed to reinforce a message that has been repeatedly -- that has repeatedly been orally conveyed to him and to his colleagues in Dvor." Do you accept that or not accept that, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer a question put in this way. You're not asking me anything specific. There are some things that I agree with but I cannot answer with a yes or a no. I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you just said that -- and your answer was a bit vague. When I asked you whether the issue was raised with you before, then you said no, not in that way, or not in the same way. Now Mr. Harmon confronts you with a letter in which Mr. Kirudja sends a copy of the letter we earlier discussed, and says that the letter is designed to reinforce a message that has repeatedly been orally conveyed to him and to his colleagues in Dvor. So Mr. Kirudja is saying I raised the issue a couple of times with Mr. Pasic. Now, do you accept that in view of your previous answer, or do you not accept that? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that there were conversations and that we did discuss this topic and that I am familiar with certain aspects of the international law and what is acceptable and what is not, but Kirudja could write whatever he wanted to write. It's his right to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not -- so do I have to understand your earlier answer to be, yes, the matter was raised at earlier conversations although perhaps not exactly in the same way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. More or less that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would have preferred to receive that answer right away instead of after three other questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, Mr. Pasic, to the transfer of Muslims that occurred on the 22nd of July 1992. Specifically, Mr. Pasic, on the 22nd of July, a large number of Muslims, as you testified earlier, left in a convoy. In July of 1992, the situation on the ground, the military situation on the ground, was stable and there were no -- the military had complete control over Bosanski Novi; is that correct? Talking about on the 15th of July, a week before the mass transfer of people. I showed you a document, I highlighted a document, you had an opportunity to review it during the recess. And I'm referring, Your Honours, to tab 26.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the situation was never under the full control. It was never safe. And that applies to the time that you're asking me about. But it was to a certain extent safer but not so safe that anybody could provide any guarantees about the matters that I've already spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to the second paragraph, the first sentence, which I will read very quickly: "Assessing the current --" This is a first -- 1 Krajina Corps report, dated the 15th of July, directed -- it's a military secret. And it is relating to the current political and security situation in the 1 KK zone of responsibility. This is signed by Colonel Milutin Vukelic. Second paragraph, first sentence, says: "Assessing the current political and security situation in SRBH, one can no longer speak of situation of crisis armed conflict and crisis spots." Bottom of page 1, starting at five lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we have established now, I think, four, five, six, seven or eight times, that Mr. Pasic's perception of what is secure, what is safe, what is militarily controlled, is -- was and is not the same as from the military commanders, and whether this is a difference of understanding of the facts or whether it's a different concept of what is secure and what is safe is still to be seen, but I don't know whether there is any need to go for the eighth, ninth or the tenth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was trying to illustrate to the Court the continuum of thinking on the part of the 1 KK in respect of the security situation because this now is further on. But let me get to the points that I'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was in this context, Mr. Pasic, that you conducted urgent negotiations with UNPROFOR in respect of the transfer of people that occurred on the 22nd of July 1992, and in your testimony, in your direct examination, you said that you had participated personally in negotiations with UN relief officials, including Jean-Claude Concolato, and that those discussions had taken place on the 18th of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were negotiations. Whether they were on the 18th of July or not, I don't know, but there were negotiations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, in those negotiations the UN relief officials, Mr. Pasic, wanted the Muslims to be able to return to their homes and you refused.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the Muslims wanted to return to their homes? Is that what you said? Have I understood your question properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I said that the UN relief officials wanted the Muslims to be able to be returned to their homes, and you refused. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in a position to refuse anything like that. That didn't come under my competence. I just spoke about the situation, and I proposed to the people from the UN, the representatives of the commissioner, that they should talk to the Muslim representatives and the families of people where we would not be present so that they could convince themselves of the actual state of affairs, to see whether they really did want to leave or not leave, whether they were being forced by anybody, or whether something else was happening altogether. So it was the representatives, and Mr. Jensen, I think his name was, Jean-Claude, the other man, that these people -- and there was a third man, I don't remember his name -- they were the ones that talked to me mostly, and they became convinced, I think - and some people could confirm this - by the -- on the Muslim side. That they were convinced that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I take it that you have some document you can present that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll finish, because even if I take off the time I used, then we are well over the ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, this is my last series of questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Pasic, you refused the UN officials the opportunity to meet with the Muslims. That's the case, isn't it, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I asked -- I precisely asked them to ask to talk to the Muslims. Not that I refused. I was the initiator of a talk like that, that they should talk to them without my presence, without any subjectivity on the part and in my person, if they had any suspicions there. So I personally insisted that they themselves should talk to the Muslims themselves, without my presence, and I repeat that. So the question was put topsy-turvy. How it was was as I've just described it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could return Your Honours' attention to the document that's found in tab 27. Mr. Pasic, tab 27, there is a document. I'm going to read portions of it to you, Mr. Pasic. It relates to those discussions that you had with Mr. Jean-Claude Concolato. This is an Associated Press article, dated -- from Zagreb, dated July 29th, and I'll read this to you, Mr. Pasic. "The United Nations was coerced into taking part in the ethnic cleansing of a Bosnian city last week when Serbs threatened harm to Muslims kept in a ghetto surrounded by guards, a UN official said Wednesday. Jean-Claude Concolato harshly criticisd Serbian authorities in the northern city of Bosanski Novi as he prepared to leave the office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees in Zagreb, which he has led since December 1991. 'We have been forced to take part in this monstrous policy of ethnic cleansing,' Concolato said in an interview with Associated Press. On July 23rd some 7.000 panicked Muslims left Bosanski Novi with a population of about 40.000 in a UN organised convoy with only the few belongings they could carry. They arrived in Karlovac, Croatia, where many of them were taken in by Germany. When Concolato went to Bosanski Novi on July 18th, he wanted to ensure that the Muslims could stay in the homes which their families had held for generations. He said he attempted to negotiate such an arrangement with the city's Serbian mayor but the local authorities made it clear that the Muslims could be in danger if they remained, Concolato said. On the next day, a Muslim was killed by an unidentified gunman, and the following night there were two explosions near the ghetto. 'I realised that those incidents were an element in the negotiations,' with the Serb-dominated local authorities, said Concolato. The Bosanski Novi mayor, who Concolato identified as Pasic, 'kept repeating that if we did not take care of these people, if we did not take them out, we, the United Nations, would be responsible for bad things that could happen to them,' he said. Concolato said that Pasic refused to guarantee the security of the Muslims on the grounds that a civil war was going on. He also said -- he said he also was refused permission to spend the night with the Muslim community. 'I realised that we had been trapped and blackmailed,' said Concolato. He said that the ghetto was guarded by uniformed soldiers and that the roads into the corridor were blocked. He was unsure whether Muslims had been forced into the ghetto or if they had gathered there voluntarily. 'I realised probably the next step would be like in Sarajevo, to send in a few shells on them,' said Concolato. 'There was a clear will to continue the policy of ethnic cleansing.'" That, Mr. Pasic, is the perception of Mr. Concolato, your interlocutor in those negotiations. What do you say to his account?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His alleged account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it is alleged account. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, his alleged account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is hearsay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I asked you to comment on that account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see whether you -- it appears already from a previous answer, that what the Chamber would expect, in view of what we have listened to carefully, that you would deny the truth of what was said in this newspaper article. If that's the case, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Mr. Concolato wrote, and I don't remember this. The text is rather a lengthy one for me to be able to answer in one sentence, but there were talks. Now, whether the UN committed ethnic cleansing, I don't know. That's what Mr. Concolato said. I can't say one way or another. I know what I myself did. I know how much I worked and how much effort I put in to help those people. Now, how this was assessed by the UN people is up to them. It's their subjective assessment. Now, whether this was written in such a way as to deal with one's own dirty linen or to rid themselves of the blame, I don't know. I know what happened and I've said what happened many times before this Tribunal. I spoke about these negotiations and said that the intentions were really honest. I see that there are some doubts, but I myself and the Crisis Staff really did want to help those people sincerely and to ensure that those who wanted to leave could leave in a civilised and dignified manner, and that's what we asked the High Commissioner for Refugees to do, or rather, the UN representatives that we've just mentioned. Now, what their views and assessment of the situation was is not for me to comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, this -- I take it this was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have one exhibit that I would like. It's a new exhibit, it's found at tab 31 and could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to finish with this witness. If it's a contextual exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You could make it a contextual exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then see whether it can be introduced and then please inform Mr. Josse about it, and we will have the break as short as possible. That means, if possible, 20 minutes. Then, Mr. Josse, with the assistance of the interpreters and -- I would like to finish today, even if it would be a couple of minutes later than a quarter to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may pass up a detailed map of the city of Bosanski Novi, which also shows the football stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We asked for that and I take it that such a map isn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll deal with that in my re-examination, and I'm grateful to the Prosecution for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, if possible, the Chamber, in order to make -- move things quickly, would there be any objection if the Chamber would have already a look at this rather neutral document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very good idea, if I might respectfully say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Then we'll have a break until 20 minutes past one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, we've all had a chance look at the map. The football stadium is at the bottom left-hand corner, number 10. There is another one. Excellent. Yes, I can see your finger is in the right place. My only question is, bearing in mind the various questions that you were asked by Mr. Harmon, and also by the learned Presiding Judge, does that help you at all as to the visibility that's been alleged by some previous witnesses - or at least one witness - in this case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this isn't what I drew, but yes, it's the right drawing and I wanted to explain this curve in the river Una. If we look at the right-hand side, the white is a flat area and part of Croatia, and the other side is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We haven't got the map in front of us any more at this moment, and at the same time we don't have the picture. Perhaps we -- could the photograph that was P183, I think, be put on the ELMO again so that we know what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's, for my part --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Go on, Mr. Pasic, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at the stalls, it's the left-hand side in the map. That's the left-hand side. I think this left-hand part, there is a branch of the river Una and a small island there on the left-hand side, the Croatian side. Well, there is a sort of wooded area, not a real forest or wood but quite tall trees, on both sides of the river Una, and along the banks on both sides there are trees, a wood. So this is flat land here, all the white space. I don't know how many metres, but, of course, you could measure this and look at the scale of the map, which will tell you how big this flat land is on the left-hand side of the Una, and then afterwards, you get the hills - not very high hills - if we are talking about the left-hand side, the left bank of the river Una in Croatia, that's it. Is that enough? Is that sufficient? Or do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't got any more questions on this subject. I don't know whether the Bench has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear what the witness tells us at this moment. The green patch we talked about before, just above the head of the lady, looking at the map, is it still your testimony that this is on Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this: If we look at it from this side, that would be more visible and clearer. If it's this area here where the town itself is located or across town, then it's about seven or eight to ten kilometres and some hills behind, which might be in this part too, downstream from town, or possibly it is the hills on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it still -- is it still Republika Srpska or does the map change your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't changed my mind. I'm just trying to think realistically as far as is possible. Well, I don't know what side this was taken from, whether it was taken from top to bottom or from some other side. It's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what makes it difficult to say? How could it be on both sides? Could it be anything else but on the left side as on my sketch of the football ground? Would you expect the spectators to look away from the football? Is there any disagreement between the parties? Mr. Josse? Is it -- will it be part of the Defence case that this green patch is on the Republika Srpska territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to help. I mean that being as helpful as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then let's move on. Perhaps Mr. -- No, let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to change the subject completely, please, Mr. Pasic -- sorry. I want to change the subject completely, please, Mr. Pasic, and I want to ask you about something you were first questioned in relation to at the start of your cross-examination last year, and that's the document variant A and B, found at tab 38 of the exhibit bundle. Could you turn to tab 38, please. You don't have it in front of you. I think you had given evidence to the effect that you had seen this document previously, sometime in 1991-1992. Do you recall when you first saw it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that last time, that I can't be sure when I first saw it, although I am acquainted with the document but I can't give you a date. If I were to give you a date I would be lying because I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of being at a meeting in Sarajevo where it was handed out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that and said that I don't remember. There was discussion about that issue last time. I really can't remember whether at that meeting at the Holiday Inn hotel that happened or not. I can't remember. I went to the Holiday Inn for meetings but privately as well, quite apart from any politics for certain matters, so I knew the Holiday Inn hotel, but I can't remember whether I attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to what extent did it play a part, if at all, in the way you administered Novi Grad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't play any part at all, more or less, if I can put it that way. And as I said, in mid-April, roughly mid-April, the Crisis Staff was established in 1992, and if you look at when this was brought in, we didn't work according to these instructions or guidelines, because before all those events, the authorities were functioning, and I said that the majority power was held by the majority Serb population that lived there, so in this division of power with the SDA, we received votes, percentage-wise, at the elections that were held in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could you turn now to tab 5, which is P1025. A section of this document was shown to you on the last occasion, or was put to you, to be more accurate, on the last occasion. I want to take you through one or two other parts of it, please. The second paragraph, which says, "In view of its geographic and strategic position, Bosanski Novi has become interesting to all of the warring parties, i.e., wartime and ideological opponents. The extremist part of the SDA has proceeded to issue arms on a massive scale to citizens of Muslim ethnicity prepared primarily to execute any tasks entrusted to them by the SDA." Is that a true comment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I might be allowed to look at this part - I don't know whose report this is, probably a free interpretation - yes, it did exist. There was weaponry on -- on the part of the Muslim population, and the SDA did have weapons before the conflict, and you could see this. When the groups were disarmed, they did have army weapons, but as I've already said, that part was done by the army, or rather, the TO staff and the police. I did not take part in those events but I was informed and probably some of those people could be better placed to tell you how much weaponry was found and where and who was in charge of the weapons, because I really didn't focus on that aspect because it didn't come under my remit, but according to the responsible persons, there was this weaponry that was in the hands of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, there are a number of names of people involved in paramilitary Muslim activity. Reading those names to yourself, can you comment as to whether you have any knowledge as to the truth of the assertions so far as those names are concerned.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me repeat, the information that I received and according to it, it was these people first, and the security services informed us that they were the people who were the main actors and protagonists of that type of weaponry for those units and formations. So the people enumerated here, mentioned here, are the same ones that I was led to believe did that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau was wondering about the origin of this document, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon dealt with that on the last occasion. I would have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's in the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have overlooked that, then I apologise and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 10, please. First page. I want to deal with the sentence in the middle of paragraph number 3, immediately after it says, in your language, [B/C/S spoken], the sentence after that reads, "There have been no armed conflicts in this territory, but the situation is extremely tense." This document is dated the 15th of May of 1992. Is it true that there had been no armed conflicts in the territory prior to the 15th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this, whether this was done by General Talic and what he meant when he said "armed conflict." In my view, an armed conflict begins when the first bullet is fired. I spoke about that situation. During the night between the 10th and the 11th, the military police was attacked in the village of Blagaj. I don't think I have to go over that again. If I have to, I will. But it was already then that an armed conflict started. What the author of this text meant when he said "armed conflict," I don't know. I don't know what he meant. Maybe he had in mind a large-scale conflict, but this is just my subjective view.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 11, please. This is a lengthy report for the public security station at Bosanski Novi. On page 2 in both languages, in your version it's the sentence that is immediately before the paragraph that begins 9th of June 1992. And the sentence in the preceding paragraph says: "During their stay in the reception centre, the citizens had sports and social rooms of the football club available and they were supplied with water and food on a regular basis." You've already told us that was the information that was relayed to you, so far as the people in the stadium were concerned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I've already said twice or three times. I said how this was secured and how they were supplied with food and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you, please, to have a look at a document that we saw for the first time today, which is now P1030. The Prosecution have got, Your Honour, what isn't so much the original but is the original copy, so to speak. Again, Mr. Harmon is anxious that that document doesn't become part of the court record. I have no problem with that but I'd like the witness to have a look at it, please. You told us earlier, Mr. Pasic, that you did not think your signature appeared at number 11. Looking at that version, is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that this was not my signature. I said that I was not in Korcanica and I'm 100 per cent sure of that. I was never in Korcanica. I don't know whether I was there before the war. I don't think so. I believe that this is my handwriting, but I have doubts about this list. I don't know whether somebody added the lines that are on top of that page, or maybe this is from another meeting. I said that I was at meetings in Sanski Most. Those were regional meetings. Those were just briefings without any legal power. We were just given information as to what was happening in the territory of the municipality and the two neighbouring municipalities. What I'm saying is that I was not in Korcanica. I never claimed that under number 11, that this is not my first name and my last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read the report of the meeting in Korcanica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask, the last line of the last answer of the witness was "I never claimed that under number 11, that this is not my first name and my last name," but about the signature, is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is it your handwriting? Is number 11 your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... confused about name and signature before and now first name and last name, which -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at the minutes of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I did read these minutes. I don't know when.
